source_name: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025 (AI trust section)
publication_date: Fielded 2025, results published starting July 29, 2025 (main report); follow-on 'leaders' analysis and blog coverage ran through October 2025 and into early 2026.
methodology_type: Self-report survey, attitude data. Over 49,000 responses from 177 countries on the full survey; the AI-accuracy-trust question specifically drew 33,244 responses (a 67.8% response rate against those who saw that question). No telemetry or behavioral/commit data backs the trust figures, only stated attitudes.
sample_size: 49,000+ total respondents across 177 countries; 33,244 responses to the AI-trust-in-accuracy question specifically. Recruitment is Stack Overflow's standard annual survey panel (site visitors and community outreach), not a controlled random sample.
pct_distrust_ai_code: 46% actively distrust the accuracy of AI tool output (26.1% 'somewhat distrust' + 19.6% 'highly distrust'), up from 31% in 2024. Only 33% trust it overall (29.6% 'somewhat trust' + 3.1% 'highly trust'). [uncertain] The task note's framing of 'trust fell to 29%' appears to reference the 'somewhat trust' slice (29.6%) alone rather than total trust (33%); total trust fell from a prior-year figure that is itself reported inconsistently across secondary sources as either about 40% or 43%, so the exact prior-year baseline could not be pinned to one number in the sources reviewed.
pct_always_verify: [uncertain] Not directly asked as an 'always verify before committing' question. Closest proxies: 45% of respondents say debugging AI-generated code is time-consuming, and only 4.4% believe AI handles complex tasks 'very well' (39.6% say it performs poorly to very poorly on complex work), implying most developers report needing to check AI output but the survey does not quantify a discrete 'always check' behavior the way the Qodo/Sonar surveys do.
stated_behavioral_gap: [uncertain] Stack Overflow does not compute a distrust-vs-verification gap in the same terms as the Qodo/Sonar pair; its closest structural finding is the adoption/trust paradox itself: AI tool usage rose to 84% of developers (from 76% in 2024) in the same year trust fell, i.e. usage keeps climbing while stated trust falls, which is an adoption-trust gap rather than a trust-verification gap.
verification_behavior_detail: The survey frames the cost of low trust mainly as debugging time rather than a discrete checking ritual: 45% call debugging AI-generated code time-consuming, and complex-task performance is rated poorly by 39.6% of respondents (only 4.4% rate it 'very well'). It does not break down specific verification methods (running tests, manual line-by-line reading, static analysis tooling) the way this project's fields ask for.
seniority_breakdown: Experienced professional developers show the most distrust: developers with 10+ years' experience report 2.5% 'highly trust' (the lowest of any group) and 20.7% 'highly distrust' (the highest). Professional developers overall land at 2.7% highly trust / 19.7% highly distrust. Early-career/learning-to-code respondents are comparatively more trusting: about 3% highly trust and 17.5% highly distrust. This matches the task note's claim that senior/experienced developers show the most distrust; the exact figure in the note (2.6% highly trust) sits between the 2.5% (10+ years) and 2.7% (professional developers overall) figures found here rather than matching either exactly. [uncertain] flagging the precise 2.6% figure as not independently reproduced, though the direction and rough magnitude of the pattern are confirmed.
culture_incentive_angle: [uncertain] Materials reviewed do not attribute the trust decline to career risk, blame allocation, or deadline pressure. The stated frustrations are output quality ('almost right, but not quite') and debugging time cost, which are product-quality complaints rather than organizational-incentive explanations.
measured_proxy_angle: [uncertain] Not addressed in the material reviewed. The survey does not discuss a leadership-side metric (velocity, PR throughput, feature count) that would discourage verification time; its focus is individual developer sentiment, not organizational measurement systems.
human_factors_parallel: [uncertain] No parallel to a non-software human-factors domain (aviation, radiology, automation bias literature) found in the Stack Overflow material reviewed.
leadership_implication: Limited to a vendor-style recommendation rather than a management practice: then-CEO Prashanth Chandrasekar is quoted saying an approach 'that leans heavily on trustworthy, responsible use of data from curated knowledge bases is critical,' positioning Stack Overflow's own community-vetted content as the fix for AI's trust problem. No explicit guidance for engineering managers on review process, staffing, or incentives was found in the material reviewed.
methodological_caveat: This is an opt-in community survey (Stack Overflow's own site visitors and community), not a random or representative sample of all developers, so the trust figures may skew toward respondents already engaged with the Stack Overflow ecosystem. The precise prior-year trust baseline (40% vs. 43% cited across different secondary write-ups) was not resolved to a single authoritative figure from the pages reviewed, and the 2.6%-highly-trust figure in the task's own note was not found verbatim; the closest confirmed figures are 2.5% (10+ years experience) and 2.7% (professional developers overall).
